title: Prototype
description: Prototype development covers pilot models built to resolve technical uncertainty before commercial production under the IRC Section 41 R&D credit.
summary: Prototype development under the federal R&D tax credit (IRC Section 41) covers pilot models built to resolve technical uncertainty before commercial production. For U.S. taxpayers, consumed prototype materials, related wages, and 65% of eligible contract research can qualify, but materials in prototypes the taxpayer capitalizes and depreciates, and activities after commercial readiness, are excluded.

body.text: Prototype development under the federal R&D tax credit (IRC Section 41) covers pilot models built to resolve technical uncertainty before commercial production. For U.S. taxpayers, consumed prototype materials, related wages, and 65% of eligible contract research can qualify, but materials in prototypes the taxpayer capitalizes and depreciates, and activities after commercial readiness, are excluded.
Executive Summary: The Prototype Nexus in Federal Research Tax Law

Within the statutory and administrative architecture of the United States Research and Development (R&D) Tax Credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41), the development, testing, and iterative refinement of a prototype serve as the primary evidentiary anchor for substantiating qualified research. While the statutory text of IRC Section 41 does not contain a standalone lexical definition of the word "prototype," the eligibility chain under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i) directly incorporates the research and experimental expenditure rules of IRC Section 174 (and IRC Section 174A for domestic research or experimental expenditures following the enactment of Public Law 119-21) and Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4)—as finalized by Treasury Decision (T.D.) 9680—and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Large Business and International (LB&I) Directive for Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) 730, federal tax law explicitly governs preliminary models, simulations, and representations through the regulatory construct of a "pilot model". Within this authoritative framework, a prototype (or pilot model) encompasses any physical article, preliminary model, fully functional representation, digital simulation, or experimental trial build of a product or component constructed during the research cycle to evaluate technical alternatives and resolve uncertainty regarding a business component—defined statutorily under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B) to include any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business.

The strategic and financial significance of rigorous prototype classification stems from its dual role in federal tax compliance. First, from a qualitative standpoint, the iterative lifecycle of a prototype—spanning initial hypothesis generation, design specification, physical or digital fabrication, destructive or performance validation testing, failure analysis, and engineering redesign—directly satisfies the most heavily scrutinized prongs of the statutory Four-Part Test under IRC Section 41(d)(1) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a): the elimination of technological uncertainty concerning capability, method, or appropriate design, and the execution of a systematic process of experimentation grounded in the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Second, from a quantitative standpoint, properly bounded prototyping activities unlock substantial Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) across the statutory expenditure categories of IRC Section 41(b): in-house qualified wages under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(i), in-house qualified supplies under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), eligible computer time-sharing or cloud computing expenses under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(iii), and third-party contract research expenses (CREs) under IRC Section 41(b)(3). Because tangible raw materials and component parts used or consumed during experimental prototype fabrication and destructive testing—or incorporated into pilot models and experimental molds whose ownership transfers to customers without being depreciated by the taxpayer, as established in TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009)—are 100% includable as qualified supply expenses under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C), accurate classification prevents experimental material costs from being improperly defaulted into non-creditable Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) or excluded depreciable fixed asset accounts.

At the same time, prototype expenditures represent a primary focal point of IRS examination and appellate litigation, particularly within custom manufacturing, shipbuilding, automotive tooling, aerospace, medical device fabrication, and software engineering. Administrative guidance—including the IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e. Research Tax Credit) IRC § 41 (Research Credit ATG), the Audit Guidelines on the Application of the Process of Experimentation for All Software (Software ATG), the Aerospace Industry Research Credit Audit Techniques Guide, and the heightened business-component reporting mandate in Section G of Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities, mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025 unless a small-filer or payroll-credit exception applies)—requires taxpayers to demarcate the exact boundary where experimental prototyping ends and commercial production begins. Under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(A) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2), once a prototype or business component is developed to the point where it is ready for commercial sale or use, or satisfies the taxpayer's basic functional and economic requirements, subsequent activities—including preproduction planning, tooling up for production, trial production runs, accumulating production process data, troubleshooting production equipment faults, and debugging post-readiness flaws—are statutorily excluded from the research credit.
Statutory and Regulatory Framework Governing Prototypes
Reconciling the Statutory Text and Regulatory Pilot Model Construct

A rigorous technical analysis of prototype qualification requires resolving an apparent definitional tension frequently encountered in practitioner literature regarding the statutory and regulatory treatment of prototypes. While general statutory commentary notes that IRC Section 41 does not explicitly define the word "prototype," technical summaries of the Treasury Regulations reference an explicit legal definition of a prototype as a "pilot model" created to evaluate a component's design or resolve technical uncertainty. Both statements reflect distinct, complementary layers of the federal tax hierarchy that operate through an explicit statutory cross-reference rather than a substantive conflict.

At the statutory level, the text of IRC Section 41 establishes the overarching framework for "qualified research" under IRC Section 41(d) and "qualified research expenses" under IRC Section 41(b) without enumerating a standalone lexical definition for "prototype". However, the first statutory prong of qualified research under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A)—and its implementing provision in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i)—mandates that qualified research must be research with respect to which expenditures may be treated as research or experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174 (or domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174A following the enactment of Public Law 119-21, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act), explicitly directing taxpayers to Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2.

At the regulatory level, Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4)—promulgated in final form by T.D. 9680 (79 FR 42195, effective July 21, 2014)—bridges this statutory generality by codifying the definition of a "pilot model":

For purposes of this section, the term pilot model means any representation or model of a product that is produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during the development or improvement of the product. The term includes a fully-functional representation or model of the product or a component of the product.

Furthermore, the IRS LB&I Directive (Guidance for Allowance of the Credit for Increasing Research Activities under IRC Section 41 for Taxpayers that Expense Research and Development Costs on their Financial Statements pursuant to ASC 730) formally equates the two terms for examination purposes, defining "Prototype" (also referred to as a Pilot Model) by direct incorporation of Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4). Under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(1), costs incurred to construct and test a pilot model remain eligible even if paid or incurred after physical production begins, provided they are incurred before uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of the product is eliminated; moreover, the ultimate success, failure, sale, or internal use of the pilot model does not disqualify the underlying experimental expenditures. Where an overall product is already established and technical uncertainty is confined to a specific subassembly, the parallel "shrinking-back" provisions of Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(5) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2) narrow the pilot model and qualified research analysis to the specific experimental component or subcomponent undergoing development, as illustrated in Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(11), Examples 3 through 8. Consequently, for federal tax administration, a prototype is not merely an informal engineering draft or a routine commercial first-article sample; it is the physical or digital embodiment of an experimental hypothesis constructed to validate design parameters prior to commercial readiness.
The Four-Part Statutory Test Applied to Prototyping

To qualify prototype-related employee labor, raw materials, computer simulation time, and third-party contractor costs as eligible QREs, the underlying activities must constitute Qualified Research Activities (QRAs) by satisfying all four prongs of the statutory test under IRC Section 41(d)(1) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a). Under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(A) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(6), these four tests must be applied separately to each discrete business component. The physical or digital existence of a prototype provides the auditable nexus linking incurred expenditures to the statutory and regulatory criteria detailed in the table below.

cells: 1. Permitted Purpose (Business Component Test)

The activity must be intended to discover information useful in the development of a new or improved business component (product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used in the taxpayer's trade or business) that relates to a qualified purpose: a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality (excluding style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors).

The prototype serves as the testable medium through which targeted functional, structural, mechanical, or algorithmic improvements are physically or digitally evaluated against baseline engineering specifications. If the overall system fails to qualify as a whole, the analysis shrinks back to the specific prototype subassembly or component under experimentation.
IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), IRC § 41(d)(2)(A)–(C), IRC § 41(d)(3)(A)–(B), and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(2)(ii), (a)(5)(ii) & (b)(2).
2. Technological in Nature (Discovering Information Test)

The process of experimentation used to discover information must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Taxpayers may employ existing technologies and rely on established scientific or engineering principles; the regulations do not require obtaining knowledge that exceeds the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the field.

Prototype design, fabrication, and validation testing apply hard-science principles—such as metallurgy, polymer chemistry, thermodynamics, structural mechanics, electrical engineering, or computational algorithm architecture—to evaluate performance. Issuance of a utility patent under 35 U.S.C. § 151 (other than a design patent under 35 U.S.C. § 171) serves as conclusive evidence that this prong is met.
IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i)–(iii) & (a)(4) (as finalized in T.D. 9104).
3. Elimination of Technological Uncertainty (Section 174 / 174A Test)

Expenditures must qualify under IRC § 174 / IRC § 174A as research or experimental costs incurred to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component. Uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the component, or the appropriate design of that component.

The decision to construct a pilot model or prototype confirms that existing engineering knowledge available to the taxpayer cannot guarantee whether a component can be built (capability), how it can be fabricated (method), or what exact specifications or geometries are required (appropriate design).
4. Process of Experimentation ("Substantially All" Test)

Substantially all (80% or more, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis) of the research activities for each business component must constitute elements of a systematic process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where capability, method, or appropriate design is uncertain at the outset.

Iterative prototyping—spanning CAD modeling, simulation, physical or digital build of Prototype Versions 1.0 through V4.0, stress testing, failure analysis, and engineering redesign—embodies systematic evaluation of alternatives. For physical pilot models, production costs incurred to resolve design uncertainty must satisfy the 80% activity fraction.
IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) & (a)(6), and Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023).

body.text: The Three Functional Pillars of a Tax-Qualified Prototype

Synthesizing the statutory prongs of IRC Section 41(d) with Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4), IRS Audit Techniques Guides, and federal appellate jurisprudence yields three operational pillars that distinguish a tax-qualified prototype from standard commercial inventory or routine custom fabrication.

First, the prototype must be initiated to achieve the resolution of specific technical uncertainties—such as whether a structural geometry can withstand target operating pressures, whether a custom vessel design will achieve functional specifications, or whether a software architecture can process transactions within target latency thresholds—where the outcome cannot be known in advance based on publicly available information or standard engineering practice available to the taxpayer. As Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) clarifies, uncertainty regarding the appropriate design of a business component is sufficient to warrant a process of experimentation even if the taxpayer already knows it has the capability and method to manufacture the product generally. However, as the Tax Court emphasized in Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, and Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, merely designing custom-engineered systems to meet client specifications does not transform every bespoke commercial build into a qualifying pilot model where detailed design parameters are established prior to fabrication without genuine technological uncertainty.

Second, the construction and testing of the unit must occur within a systematic evaluation of alternatives involving modeling, simulation, or structured trial-and-error methodology that compares competing design hypotheses (for instance, evaluating Hypothesis A against Hypothesis B, or sequentially testing iterative design modifications). Critically, under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(6) and the Seventh Circuit's ruling in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), aff'g T.C. Memo. 2021-15, simply labeling a first-in-class vessel or custom machine a "pilot model" does not automatically carry the entire unit through the Fourth Prong. Rejecting the looser "novelty" or "feels new enough" approach previously applied by the district court in Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States, 691 F. Supp. 2d 688 (N.D. Tex. 2010), aff'd in part and vacated and remanded in part, 757 F.3d 400 (5th Cir. 2014), the Seventh Circuit held that while physical pilot model production expenses are included in the denominator of the "substantially all" fraction—and may also be included in the numerator when the physical model is constructed specifically to test and resolve developmental uncertainty—the taxpayer must substantiate on an activity-by-activity basis that at least 80% of the research activities for that business component (or shrunk-back subcomponent) constituted elements of a process of experimentation.

Third, the unit must possess an evaluative primary purpose at the time of its fabrication. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(1) and (a)(11), Example 7, as well as the Tax Court's holding in TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009), a pilot model or experimental prototype does not lose its research character merely because it is fully functional, is subsequently used as a demonstration model, or is ultimately sold to a customer after experimentation concludes. However, as the Seventh Circuit observed in Little Sandy Coal, "the creator's intent matters" under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4): the primary purpose of constructing the model during development must be technical evaluation and uncertainty resolution rather than the routine manufacture of commercial inventory lacking design risk.
The Evidentiary Value of Prototype Failure and Destructive Testing

A critical analytical takeaway for IRS audit defense is the counter-intuitive evidentiary superiority of failed prototypes over immediate commercial successes. Both Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) and Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(1) explicitly establish that qualified research eligibility does not require the taxpayer to succeed in developing a new or improved business component. Nevertheless, when a taxpayer presents only a single, successful commercial build during an IRS examination—particularly where testing occurred only at the very end of fabrication for routine acceptance verification, as in Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84—examiners and courts frequently challenge whether genuine technological uncertainty existed at the outset of the project or whether the testing was merely excluded quality control inspection under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i).

Conversely, when Prototype 1.0 or Prototype 2.0 fails during performance validation or intentional destructive stress testing—or when a subcomponent fails during a quality control test due to an inappropriate design and requires $8,000 of engineering reconfiguration and retesting, as explicitly illustrated in Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(11), Example 4—the resulting failure analysis reports, scrap logs, and Engineering Change Orders (ECOs) provide contemporaneous, objective evidence that initial design parameters were uncertain and required systematic iteration. Documenting the precise physical, mechanical, chemical, or algorithmic failure modes encountered between iterative builds transforms engineering setbacks into compelling legal substantiation for the research credit.
Categorizing and Substantiating Prototype-Related Expenditures (QREs)

Under IRC Section 41(b)(1), Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) are defined as the sum of "in-house research expenses" under IRC Section 41(b)(2) and "contract research expenses" under IRC Section 41(b)(3) paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the taxable year in carrying on a trade or business. As Chapter 4 of the IRS Research Credit ATG underscores, if an expenditure is not specifically enumerated in IRC Section 41(b), a taxpayer may not claim it as a QRE. Prototype development generates eligible expenditures across the statutory QRE categories: qualified supplies under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and (C), qualified wages under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and (B), eligible computer rental or cloud simulation expenses under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(4), and third-party contract research expenses under IRC Section 41(b)(3). Each category is governed by specific statutory inclusion rates—100% for qualified in-house wages, qualified supplies consumed in research, and eligible computer use, compared to a general 65% limitation for third-party contract research (with narrow statutory tiers of 75% for payments to qualified research consortia under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(C) and 100% for eligible energy research paid to universities, federal laboratories, or eligible small businesses under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(D))—and carries distinct accounting and compliance risks that must be managed to prevent examination disallowance.
Qualified Supply Expenses: The Consumption Rule vs. Depreciable Property Risk

Under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and Section 41(b)(2)(C), qualified supply expenses encompass any tangible property used or consumed in the conduct of qualified research, expressly excluding (i) land or improvements to land, and (ii) "property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation". Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(1) specifies that supplies are used in the conduct of qualified research if they are used in the performance of qualified services by an employee of the taxpayer (or a person acting in a capacity similar to an employee). Raw materials, electronic components, chemical reagents, custom polymer blends, and metal alloys used to fabricate and test experimental prototypes fall squarely within this definition—and are 100% includable in QREs—when they are used or consumed during the development and testing process. Conversely, intangible costs, general and administrative (G&A) expenses, travel, meals, entertainment, telephone charges, relocation or lease fees, royalty or license expenses, ordinary facility utilities (absent proof of extraordinary utility consumption for high-energy research equipment under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii)), and "Prototype Overhead" (defined in the IRS ASC 730 Directive as all costs allocated to a prototype other than direct labor and direct materials) are excluded from supply QREs.

However, Chapter 4.b of the IRS Research Credit ATG explicitly instructs examiners to "carefully scrutinize 'prototype' expenditures to determine whether the 'prototype' is (or contains) property of a character subject to an allowance for depreciation". This creates a critical compliance dichotomy governed by the statutory consumption rule, the depreciable property rule under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) and Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(b)(1)–(4), and key Tax Court and appellate precedents:

items: Destructive Testing, Scrapping, and Physical Consumption: When a prototype is subjected to destructive stress testing, dismantled, or scrapped after validating design parameters, the tangible materials lack a useful economic life beyond the experiment and are neither capitalized nor depreciated by the taxpayer, allowing 100% of the direct material costs to qualify as QRE supplies under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C).

Prototypes and Experimental Tooling Sold to Customers ( TG Missouri Doctrine): Historically, the IRS contended that if a physical prototype or experimental mold was of a general type of durable property that could be depreciated by someone, its material costs were barred under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) regardless of the taxpayer's specific accounting treatment. In TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009), the U.S. Tax Court rejected the IRS's interpretation and held that the exclusion for "property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation" requires that the property specifically be depreciable property in the hands of the taxpayer claiming the credit. Where an automotive supplier incurred costs for production molds that were sold to customers after development and testing (even when the taxpayer retained physical possession of the molds to manufacture automotive parts while the customer held title and risk of loss), the molds were not depreciable property in the taxpayer's hands and their costs qualified as supply QREs. Treasury subsequently adopted the TG Missouri holding into final regulations under T.D. 9680 (Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(1) and (b)(4)), confirming that the ultimate sale of a pilot model does not disqualify the prior experimental expenditures.

Durable Prototypes Capitalized and Depreciated by the Taxpayer: Conversely, if a taxpayer constructs a durable, functional prototype or experimental machine and subsequently retains ownership and places it into service in its own trade or business as an internal multi-year production asset, a long-term capitalized demonstration unit, or equipment subject to an allowance for depreciation on the taxpayer's books (as TG Missouri did for the internal molds it owned and depreciated), the physical component materials assume a depreciable character in the taxpayer's hands and are statutorily barred from QRE supply treatment under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) and Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(b)(1)–(4). Even in this scenario, however, the in-house engineering wages and contract research expenses incurred to design, model, and develop the experimental equipment may still qualify as QREs.

Commercial Production Inventory and Incremental Supply Standard ( Union Carbide Doctrine): If a unit is produced without technical design uncertainty solely to fulfill a routine customer order, its materials constitute routine Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) rather than qualified research supplies. Furthermore, under Union Carbide Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50 (2009), aff'd (2d Cir. 2012), when a taxpayer conducts process experiments inside its commercial manufacturing process during production runs of salable goods, raw materials that the taxpayer would have consumed anyway to manufacture commercial product for sale are excluded from supply QREs; only the incremental supply costs that would not have been incurred but for the research activity are eligible.

body.text: Qualified Wages: Direct Engagement, Supervision, and Support

Employee compensation frequently represents the largest share of a prototype-anchored R&D tax credit claim. Under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and Section 41(b)(2)(D), "wages" means taxable wages as defined in IRC Section 3401(a) (all taxable wages reported on Form W-2, Box 1, including bonuses and taxable stock option spreads attributable to grant-year qualified services per Apple Computer, Inc. v. Commissioner, 98 T.C. 232 (1992), and Sun Microsystems v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1995-69, while excluding non-taxable fringe benefits and wages taken into account for the Work Opportunity Credit under IRC Section 51(a)). Under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c), qualified services encompass three distinct functional tiers related to prototyping: the direct conduct of qualified research, the direct supervision of qualified research, and the direct support of qualified research. Direct conduct under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B)(i) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c)(1) includes time expended by engineers, scientists, designers, and software developers directly defining technical design requirements to resolve uncertainty, developing prototype specifications, performing CAD modeling or algorithmic simulations, fabricating physical or digital prototypes, executing performance and destructive validation testing, conducting failure analysis, and engineering iterative redesigns. Direct supervision under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c)(2) encompasses compensation paid to immediate, first-line technical managers—such as laboratory directors or lead engineering managers—for directly overseeing personnel engaged in hands-on prototype fabrication and testing. As both Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c)(2) and the Tax Court in Moore v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20, emphasize, direct supervision does not include general management by higher-level executives to whom first-line managers report, except to the specific extent those executives personally perform hands-on technical research or immediate supervision of researchers (as established in Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201, subject to the reasonable compensation limitation of IRC Section 174(e)). Direct support under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c)(3) covers wages paid to technicians, machinists, or laboratory staff who directly assist persons engaging in or directly supervising qualified research. Notably, both the legislative history of Section 41 (H.R. Rep. No. 97-201, at 118 (1981)) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c)(3) explicitly cite "the services of a machinist for machining a part of an experimental model used in qualified research," alongside a laboratory worker cleaning equipment used in qualified research, a clerk compiling research data, or a secretary typing laboratory result reports, as examples of qualified direct support, whereas payroll, accounting, and general janitorial services are excluded as indirect G&A overhead.

Under the flush language of IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(d)(2), if "substantially all"—defined as 80% or more—of the services performed by an employee for the taxpayer during the taxable year consist of qualified services (calculated as the ratio of hours spent on qualified services to total hours worked, excluding sick leave), then 100% of that employee's wages for the taxable year qualify as in-house research wages. If an employee's qualified time ratio is below 80%, only the actual fractional allocation of wages attributable to qualified services may be claimed under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(d)(1). To withstand IRS examination and satisfy the mandatory Section G business-component reporting rules on Form 6765, wage allocations across all three tiers should be supported by Form W-2 records, payroll registers, and granular, contemporaneous project-level time tracking that ties employee hours directly to specific business components and prototype iterations (such as "Prototype V2.0 Stress Testing") rather than unsupported departmental estimates.
Contract Research Expenses: The 65% Limitation and Risk-of-Failure Rules

When taxpayers engage external third-party specialists to assist in prototype development—such as hiring specialized machine shops for custom fabrication of experimental components or independent laboratories to execute environmental stress testing and failure analysis—those expenditures may qualify as Contract Research Expenses (CREs) under IRC Section 41(b)(3) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e). Unlike in-house wages and supplies, which are eligible at 100%, third-party CREs are generally statutorily limited to 65% of the amounts paid or incurred for qualified research or services that, if performed by the taxpayer's own employees, would constitute qualified services under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(A) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(1). Higher statutory inclusion rates apply in two narrow contexts: 75% for amounts paid to a tax-exempt qualified research consortium under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(C) and 100% for qualified energy research paid to an eligible small business, university, or federal laboratory under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(D). Furthermore, under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(B) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(4), any prepaid contract research attributable to prototype work conducted after the close of the taxable year is treated as paid or incurred only in the taxable year in which the research is actually performed, and under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(F), any contractor research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States is excluded.

Evaluating third-party prototype contracts requires carefully separating two distinct legal doctrines that are frequently conflated in general compliance summaries: the Outbound Contract Research Eligibility Test and the Inbound Funded Research Exclusion:

items: Outbound Contract Research Eligibility (IRC § 41(b)(3) & Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)–(3)): Where the taxpayer is the payor/client hiring an external vendor or contractor to perform prototype fabrication or testing, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2) establishes a mandatory three-part test. The expense qualifies as a CRE only to the extent paid or incurred pursuant to an agreement (usually in writing) that: (i) is entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research (§ 1.41-2(e)(2)(i)); (ii) provides that the research be performed on behalf of the taxpayer (§ 1.41-2(e)(2)(ii) and (e)(3), meaning the taxpayer has a right to the research results, though exclusive rights are not required); and (iii) requires the taxpayer to bear the expense even if the research is not successful (§ 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii)). As Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2) and Example 4 of § 1.41-2(e)(5) state explicitly, if payment (or a bonus portion of a payment) to the vendor is contingent on the success of the research—such as paying a vendor only upon delivery and acceptance of a working prototype—that payment is considered paid for the product or result rather than for the performance of research, and is disallowed as a CRE to the payor.

Inbound Funded Research Exclusion (IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) & Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1)–(3)): Conversely, where a customer or government entity pays the taxpayer (acting as the performing researcher/contractor) to develop a custom prototype, IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) excludes the research as "funded research" unless the taxpayer satisfies a two-pronged test established under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d) and federal case law (Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States (Fed. Cir. 1995); Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000); GeoSynTec; Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner; and Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50). Specifically, the performing researcher's prototype work is non-funded only if: (i) the researcher bears the economic risk of failure because the customer's payment to the researcher is contingent on the success of the research under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(1), and (ii) the researcher retains substantial rights in the results of the research under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(2) (meaning the right to use the research results in its own trade or business without paying for the privilege, though exclusive rights are not required). Notably, as Chapter 5 of the IRS Research Credit ATG warns, if a contractor builds a prototype under a contingent-payment contract (so the contractor bears the financial risk) but does not retain substantial rights in the research, neither the contractor nor the person paying for the research is eligible to claim the credit: the paying customer fails the outbound risk test under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii), and the contractor fails the inbound substantial-rights test under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(2).

body.text: Hypothetical Worked Example: Quantifying Prototype QREs Across Expenditure Tiers

To illustrate the exact mechanics of these statutory rates and exclusions, consider a hypothetical medical or industrial engineering firm incurring $100,000 in qualified in-house engineering wages while developing three iterative physical prototypes (Versions V1.0 through V3.0). In addition to in-house labor, the firm spends $100,000 on raw materials (metals, sensors, and custom polymers) consumed during destructive testing of V1.0 and V2.0, and pays $20,000 to an independent domestic testing laboratory for environmental stress testing under a prior written, non-contingent research services contract where the firm bears the financial risk of failure and retains rights to the results.

body.text: Step-by-step verification of the hypothetical calculations confirms the sensitivity of the credit to supply substantiation, third-party contract structuring, and capitalization treatment:

items: Scenario 1 (Labor Only Baseline): When $100,000 of experimental prototype raw materials are unsubstantiated or misclassified into routine commercial Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) and no third-party CREs are claimed, only in-house engineering wages qualify at 100% ($100,000 × 100% = $100,000 Total QREs). At the 10% effective credit rate, the estimated net tax credit is $100,000 × 10% = $10,000.

Scenario 2 (Partial Supply Substantiation): When itemized invoices and scrap logs substantiate $50,000 of the consumed prototype materials ($50,000 × 100% = $50,000 Qualified Supplies), Total QREs increase to $100,000 (Wages) + $50,000 (Supplies) = $150,000, yielding an estimated net tax credit of $150,000 × 10% = $15,000 (a 50% increase over the labor-only baseline).

Scenario 3 (Full Supply Substantiation): When all $100,000 of destructively tested prototype materials are properly segregated and substantiated as non-depreciable supplies ($100,000 × 100% = $100,000 Qualified Supplies), Total QREs double to $100,000 (Wages) + $100,000 (Supplies) = $200,000, generating an estimated net tax credit of $200,000 × 10% = $20,000.

Scenario 4 (Full Supply Capture Plus Eligible Third-Party CRE): Adding the $20,000 non-contingent third-party laboratory testing contract applies the statutory 65% limitation under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(A) ($20,000 × 65% = $13,000 Eligible CRE). Total QREs reach $100,000 (Wages) + $100,000 (Supplies) + $13,000 (CRE) = $213,000, resulting in an estimated net tax credit of $213,000 × 10% = $21,300.

Scenario 5 (Depreciable Property Disallowance): If the taxpayer instead retains the $100,000 prototype as a durable asset, places it into service in its own trade or business, and capitalizes and depreciates it on its books, 100% of the $100,000 physical material cost is excluded from supply QREs under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) and Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(b)(1), while the $100,000 of in-house design wages and $13,000 of third-party lab testing CREs remain eligible ($100,000 + $0 + $13,000 = $113,000 Total QREs), reducing the estimated net tax credit to $113,000 × 10% = $11,300.

body.text: The Exclusionary Boundary: Prototyping Versus Commercial Production

A foundational statutory limitation under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(A) is the exclusion of any research conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component. Because the prototype lifecycle bridges conceptual engineering and manufacturing deployment, pinpointing the exact moment when experimental prototyping terminates and commercial production commences is critical for IRS examination defensibility.
Defining the Commercial Readiness Threshold

Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(i) and IRS audit guidelines, activities are conducted after the beginning of commercial production of a business component if such activities are conducted after the component is developed to the point where it is ready for commercial sale or use, or meets the basic functional and economic requirements of the taxpayer for the component's sale or use. Satisfying this functional and economic readiness threshold marks the legal termination of qualified research for that specific product business component. Even if engineering personnel continue to interact with the product after this threshold is crossed, the underlying expenditures transition from creditable R&D to excluded post-research commercialization or manufacturing overhead.

However, taxpayers and examiners must observe the statutory distinction between a product business component and a manufacturing process business component under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(C), Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(1), and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii). Under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(C), any plant process, machinery, or technique for the commercial production of a business component is treated as a separate business component from the product being produced. Accordingly, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii) explicitly provides that even after a product prototype meets the taxpayer's basic functional and economic requirements, activities relating to the development of the manufacturing process still may constitute qualified research, provided that the development of the process itself separately satisfies the requirements of IRC Section 41(d) and occurs before the manufacturing process meets the taxpayer's basic functional and economic requirements or is ready for commercial use.
Statutorily Excluded Post-Prototype Activities

Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii)(A)–(E), the legislative history to the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (H.R. Conf. Rep.), and IRS Audit Techniques Guides enumerate specific post-prototype activities that are deemed to occur after the beginning of commercial production and are strictly excluded from QREs. These non-qualifying activities encompass preproduction planning for a finished business component under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii)(A) once its design has already been validated via prototyping, such as scheduling manufacturing workflows, material procurement, or assembly-line layouts. The exclusion likewise bars expenditures for tooling up for production under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii)(B), which involves acquiring, building, or calibrating routine production-capable tooling ("rate tooling"), molds, dies, stamps, or fixtures intended to mass-produce an already-validated prototype design. By contrast, if a custom tool, mold, or robotic welding jig is itself the experimental business component (or part of an experimental production process) undergoing iterative prototyping to resolve uncertainty regarding its own capability, method, or design prior to commercial readiness, its experimental development precedes the exclusion and remains eligible until validated. Additional excluded post-prototype activities include conducting trial production runs under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii)(C) to verify throughput rates or batch consistency, troubleshooting involving the detection of faults in production equipment or manufacturing processes under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii)(D), and accumulating data relating to commercial production processes under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii)(E) (such as statistical process control metrics or routine quality control inspections under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(5)).

In heavy manufacturing and aerospace examinations, the IRS Aerospace Industry Research Credit Audit Techniques Guide maps this statutory boundary to formal engineering design milestones: design and development testing leading up to a Preliminary Design Review (PDR) and Critical Design Review (CDR)—along with pre-production Qualification Testing performed on initial engineering development units or prototypes to determine whether the item meets design and performance specifications—generally constitute qualified research, whereas activities following the Production Readiness Review (PRR), where the design is frozen and transitions to rate tooling and routine Quality Assurance/Quality Control (QA/QC) testing on selected production items, are closely scrutinized for disallowance under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(A).
Debugging Design Flaws Versus Debugging Production Flaws

One of the sharpest points of contention during IRS examinations is the treatment of "debugging" activities. Both the IRS Audit Guidelines on the Application of the Process of Experimentation for All Software (Software ATG) and regulatory rules derived from T.D. 8930 explicitly categorize "debugging flaws in a business component" after the commencement of commercial production as a non-qualifying activity under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(A). Analytical precision requires distinguishing between two fundamentally different engineering activities that often share the colloquial label "debugging".

When a physical or digital prototype fails functional validation testing prior to commercial readiness because its underlying mechanical geometry, material composition, or software algorithm architecture cannot meet required performance specifications, identifying the root cause and redesigning the component resolves technological uncertainty regarding appropriate design or capability; consequently, these pre-readiness design iteration costs remain eligible QREs. Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(11), Example 4 directly illustrates this principle: where a component of a custom machine fails during a quality control test due to the component's inappropriate design, the additional $8,000 incurred (including design retesting) to reconfigure the component's design qualifies as a research and experimental expenditure aimed at eliminating design uncertainty.

Conversely, once the final prototype successfully validates the capability, method, and appropriate design of the business component and meets basic functional and economic requirements, any subsequent effort to fix manufacturing yield drops, calibrate assembly-line tolerances, or perform corrective software maintenance—such as diagnosing and patching coding bugs, logic errors, or interface defects in minor releases (e.g., versions 1.1, 1.2, or 2.4) of an existing software product—is classified by the IRS Software ATG as "High Risk" post-readiness debugging or routine maintenance that usually fails to constitute qualified research under IRC Section 41(d). Similarly, efforts to optimize an already-validated process purely for mass-production efficiency, throughput speed, or unit cost reduction after basic functional and economic requirements have been met must cease being claimed as QREs.
Establishing Commercial Readiness for Digital Prototypes

While physical manufacturing offers tangible markers of the post-research transition—such as executing a formal Production Readiness Review, ordering production rate tooling, or reconfiguring factory floors—digital prototypes (including computer software, machine-learning algorithms, data structures, and CAD simulations) lack physical boundaries. Because modern engineering relies heavily on rapid digital prototyping and sandbox environments, establishing the exact point at which a digital prototype meets functional and economic requirements demands rigorous internal digital governance.

Furthermore, taxpayers claiming digital and software prototypes must navigate the specific software classification rules on Form 6765, Section G, Column 49(e) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(6). Under these rules, software business components must be categorized as: (A) Internal Use Software (IUS) developed primarily for internal use in general and administrative functions (financial management, human resources management, and support services), which is subject to the High Threshold of Innovation (HTI) test; (B) Dual Function Software (DFS) developed both for general and administrative functions and to enable interaction with third parties; or (C) Software Excepted from IUS Treatment, which is exempt from the HTI test and includes software developed for use in an activity that constitutes qualified research, software developed for internal use in a production process that meets the requirements of IRC Section 41(d)(1), software developed as part of a new or improved package of software and hardware, or software developed to be commercially sold, leased, licensed, or marketed to third parties or to interact with third parties.

To substantiate the commercial readiness boundary for software and digital models during an IRS examination, taxpayers should anchor their cutoff date on verifiable software lifecycle artifacts, including version control and sandbox deployment logs (such as Git commit histories demonstrating architectural experimentation in non-commercial alpha or beta builds), formal release readiness criteria defining required algorithmic accuracy or latency thresholds, and formal engineering sign-off gate documentation certifying that all core architectural uncertainties have been resolved prior to transitioning the codebase to routine user acceptance testing (UAT), vendor application configuration, or commercial deployment.
Sector-Specific Prototype Applications and Case Studies
The operational form of a prototype or pilot model varies significantly across technical domains.
Case Study 1: Advanced Medical Device Sensor Array Development

The medical device industry exemplifies multi-stage prototyping where high technical risk and strict regulatory gates generate substantial, defensible QREs. Consider a medical technology company developing a novel, portable diagnostic device centered on a proprietary internal sensor array that must operate reliably under extreme, variable biological conditions inside a compact enclosure. Under the shrinking-back rule of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2) and Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(5), even if certain outer enclosure elements use established components, the proprietary sensor array and its integrated hardware-software package constitute discrete business components. At project initiation, the engineering team confronts two primary technological uncertainties under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3): first, capability and appropriate design uncertainty regarding what specific material composition will simultaneously achieve biological compatibility and maintain structural integrity across repeated internal pressure and temperature cycles; and second, method uncertainty regarding the specialized fabrication and assembly process required to integrate the delicate sensor array into the device housing while maintaining mandatory electrical shielding without degrading structural reliability.

To resolve these uncertainties, mechanical and electrical engineers execute a three-phase process of experimentation under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5). In the initial digital prototyping phase, engineers construct digital CAD models and multiphysics simulations to evaluate candidate geometries and narrow potential material compositions, generating eligible direct engineering wages under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and eligible off-premises computer simulation costs under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(4). In the second phase, the team fabricates four sequential physical prototype generations (V1.0 through V4.0), testing distinct combinations of custom polymer blends and metal alloys alongside varying injection-molding parameters and Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machining programs. Each physical version functions as a pilot model under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4) and undergoes rigorous laboratory performance validation and destructive stress testing to identify fracture thresholds, electrical interference, and biological compliance failures. In the third phase, following iterative refinement through Prototype V4.0, the component undergoes clinical and safety testing mandated by government regulatory authorities prior to commercial release. Consistent with the regulatory framework of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iv), because regulatory approval operates as a mandatory legal and functional gate before the medical device can meet its basic functional and economic requirements for commercial sale, the costs of executing these pre-commercial clinical validation trials remain within the qualified experimentation boundary. Through this documented lifecycle, the company substantiates 100% of the raw material costs of custom polymers and alloys consumed and discarded across failed Prototypes V1.0 through V3.0 as Qualified Supplies under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C), 100% of direct engineering, first-line supervisory, and CNC machinist support labor for simulation, fabrication, destructive testing, and failure analysis as Qualified Wages under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c)(3), and 65% of amounts paid to independent domestic testing laboratories for specialized environmental and safety validation under prior, non-contingent agreements as Contract Research Expenses under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(A) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e).
Case Study 2: Custom Manufacturing Equipment and Automated Tooling

Within industrial manufacturing, taxpayers frequently struggle to distinguish excluded "tooling up for production" under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii)(B) from qualified process and equipment prototyping under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(C), Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii), and Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(11), Examples 6 and 8. Consider a manufacturer that designs a novel automated robotic welding jig to hold complex assemblies during high-speed automated welding where such specialized robotic equipment is not commercially available. When Prototype V1 of the automated jig is fabricated and tested on the shop floor, unexpected harmonic vibrations destabilize the assembly and ruin the weld integrity. Engineers perform vibration analysis, modify the structural damping geometry, integrate new feedback sensors, and fabricate Prototype V2 to test whether the revised design eliminates the harmonic distortion.

In this scenario, under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(C) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(1), the automated jig itself is a separate new or improved business component (plant machinery or process equipment used in the taxpayer's trade or business) whose appropriate design and capability to maintain positional stability under robotic welding forces were uncertain at the outset. Consequently, the engineering, machinist, and technician labor expended in designing, building, testing, and modifying Prototype V1 and Prototype V2—along with the structural steel and electronic sensors consumed and discarded in the scrapped V1 configuration—qualify as eligible QREs. However, if the final, durable Prototype V2 jig is retained by the taxpayer, placed into service in its manufacturing operations, and capitalized and depreciated on the taxpayer's books, the physical component materials of the capitalized V2 asset are excluded from supply QREs under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) and TG Missouri, 133 T.C. 278 (2009), even though the in-house engineering wages incurred to design and test V2 remain eligible QREs. Furthermore, only after the V2 jig design successfully resolves the vibration uncertainty and meets functional and economic requirements would replicating additional jigs or performing routine shop-floor calibration constitute excluded production tooling and troubleshooting under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii)(B) and (D).
Case Study 3: Fintech Software Sandbox Prototyping

In the software sector, non-commercial sandbox builds serve the exact same experimental function as physical pilot models. When a financial technology firm designs a new algorithmic architecture for real-time fraud detection intended for commercial licensing or third-party interaction (qualifying as software excepted from Internal Use Software treatment under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(6) and Form 6765, Section G, Column 49(e)), existing heuristics cannot establish whether the proposed algorithm can reduce false positives without spiking transaction latency beyond strict operational thresholds.

To evaluate competing architectural alternatives, developers construct an isolated, non-commercial "sandbox" beta build and run systematic benchmarking and back-testing simulations against historical transaction datasets. Although no physical materials are consumed, the isolated sandbox build functions as a digital prototype constructed solely to evaluate architectural alternatives under technological uncertainty pursuant to Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5). Developer wages under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and eligible third-party computer time-sharing costs under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(4) expended on coding, testing, and re-architecting the sandbox prototype qualify as QREs up to the point where the algorithm achieves target accuracy and latency thresholds for commercial deployment, distinguishing experimental development from routine post-release software maintenance and debugging.
Documentation, Substantiation, and IRS Examination Defense

The administrative and judicial environment governing IRC Section 41 has shifted decisively toward rigorous, contemporaneous project-level disclosure and substantiation. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(d) and IRC Section 6001 (Treasury Regulation § 1.6001-1), a taxpayer claiming a credit under Section 41 "must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit". As the Seventh Circuit emphasized in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), and as the Tax Court reiterated in Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, Moore v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20, and Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, general-ledger expense totals, arbitrary retrospective estimates, and uncorroborated interviews fail to satisfy the taxpayer's burden of proof—particularly regarding the requirement that at least 80% of research activities for each claimed pilot model or business component constitute a process of experimentation.

This judicial standard is reinforced on the face of the tax return by the revised Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) (Rev. December 2025, with final updated instructions released by the IRS in February 2026). Under the updated Form 6765 instructions, Section G (Business Component Information) is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 (unless filing an amended return) and becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025 (2026 and forward) unless the taxpayer qualifies for one of two specific exceptions: (1) the taxpayer is a Qualified Small Business under IRC Section 41(h)(3) (having less than $5 million in gross receipts for the tax year and no gross receipts for any tax year before the 5-tax-year period ending with the tax year) that checks the box on Form 6765 to claim a reduced payroll tax credit (up to $500,000 applied via Form 8974); or (2) the taxpayer meets the small-filer exception on an original return by having controlled-group QREs on line 48 of $1.5 million or less and average annual gross receipts under IRC Section 448(c)(3) of $50 million or less for the prior three tax years. All other filers must complete Section G under the "80%/Top 50" Business Component Rule, reporting business components in descending order by total QRE amount to account for a minimum of 80% of total QREs or a maximum of 50 business components (with any remaining components reported as a single "Aggregate Business Components" entry in Column 49(c) and Columns 50–56), while breaking down wages, supplies, computer rental costs, and contract research expenses separately for each itemized business component.
Aligning Prototype Records With the Three Core IRS Inquiries

To satisfy IRS examination standards under Chapter 7 of the Research Credit ATG (Substantiation and Recordkeeping) and Form 6765 Section G disclosures, contemporaneous prototype documentation must systematically address three foundational inquiries for each claimed business component:

items: Identification of the Business Component ("What Was Developed?"): The documentation must explicitly identify the specific product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention (or shrunk-back subcomponent under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2)) undergoing experimentation—such as "Proprietary Sensor Array – Prototype Versions V1.0 to V4.0"—matching the business component type (Product, Process, or All Others, plus software category in line 49(e) if applicable) reported in Columns 49(a)–(f) of Form 6765 Section G.

Substantiation of Qualified Research Activities ("Why Does the Activity Qualify?"): The records must demonstrate through a technical narrative, design schematics, and test logs the baseline technological uncertainty (capability, method, or appropriate design under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3) and Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4)) and the systematic process of experimentation (CAD simulations, prototype builds, destructive testing protocols, and failure analyses under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5)) executed to eliminate that uncertainty, while establishing that at least 80% of the research activities on that component constituted elements of a process of experimentation under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(6).

Quantification and Nexus of Expenditures ("How Much Did It Cost?"): The taxpayer must substantiate the claimed costs via a reconciled financial schedule linking specific employee wages, itemized material supply invoices, computer rental costs, and third-party contractor invoices in Columns 50 through 56 of Form 6765 Section G directly to that discrete prototype project.

body.text: Mapping Engineering Artifacts to Statutory Substantiation Requirements

Integrating tax substantiation directly into the engineering workflow ensures that standard technical artifacts serve as audit-ready legal evidence under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(d) and Treasury Regulation § 1.6001-1, as mapped in the table below.

cells: Technical Narratives, PDR/CDR Decks, Schematics & Design Logs
Documents baseline technical uncertainties, hard-science principles applied, and competing design hypotheses evaluated.
Permitted Purpose, Technological in Nature, & Technological Uncertainty (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)–(B), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)–(4)).
Must be recorded contemporaneously at project initiation (PDR/CDR stage) prior to resolving the uncertainty.
Test Protocols, Failure Analysis Reports & ECOs
Establishes objective pass/fail metrics, logs test failures of early builds (e.g., V1.0, V2.0), and justifies iterative engineering redesigns.
Process of Experimentation & 80% "Substantially All" Activity Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6)).
Must explicitly connect test failure metrics to subsequent Engineering Change Orders (ECOs) and separate qualification testing from routine QC.
Photographic Iteration Logs & Sandbox Git Commit Histories
Provides visual and digital evidence of physical structural or algorithmic evolution across Prototype Versions V1, V2, and V3.
Process of Experimentation & Existence of Pilot Models (Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)).
Timestamped photographs captured at each physical build and destructive test stage; tagged Git commits for software sandboxes.
Itemized Material Invoices & Scrap/Inventory Logs
Traces raw material batches to specific prototype versions and proves physical consumption, destruction, or non-depreciable disposition.
Qualified Supply Expenses: Consumption Rule vs. Capitalization (IRC § 41(b)(2)(C), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1), Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)).
Must segregate consumed experimental materials from production inventory (COGS), Prototype Overhead (ASC 730), and depreciable fixed assets.
Project-Specific Time Sheets & Payroll Registers
Substantiates the exact percentage of employee hours dedicated to hands-on prototype design, fabrication, testing, supervision, and support.
Qualified Wages: Direct Conduct, Supervision, & Support (IRC § 41(b)(2)(B), IRC § 3401(a), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)–(d)).
Granular time tracking linked to specific business component versions for Form 6765 Section G, reconciled to Form W-2 Box 1.
Third-Party Statements of Work (SOWs) & Contracts
Establishes scope of outsourced prototype fabrication/testing, intellectual property rights, domestic performance location, and allocation of financial risk.
Contract Research Expenses (65% rule under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) & Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e) & Non-Funded status under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) & Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)).
Must be executed prior to work performance, confirm domestic U.S. research (IRC § 41(d)(4)(F)), and verify that the taxpayer bears financial risk of failure and retains substantial rights.

body.text: Institutional Compliance Architecture and Actionable Governance Recommendations

To maximize eligible prototype QRE recovery while insulating claims against IRS audit adjustments and accuracy-related tax underpayment penalties (such as the 20% underpayment penalty), organizations should institutionalize formal governance controls across their engineering, procurement, legal, and accounting systems. Rather than treating R&D tax substantiation as a retrospective year-end accounting reconstruction—an approach rejected by federal courts in Little Sandy Coal, Betz, and Phoenix Design Group—companies should embed compliance checkpoints directly into their product development lifecycles.

A cornerstone of this governance architecture is institutionalizing a formal "Qualified Research Gate Review" process involving both engineering leads and R&D tax compliance specialists before any prototype is released for commercial scaling. Aligning with the Preliminary Design Review (PDR), Critical Design Review (CDR), and Production Readiness Review (PRR) milestones described in the IRS Aerospace ATG, this gate review formally documents the exact date on which the prototype satisfies basic functional and economic requirements under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(i), ensuring that 100% of legitimate experimental iterations and qualification tests prior to the gate are captured while systematically excluding post-gate preproduction planning, rate tooling, and trial production runs. Where manufacturing process development continues after the product design is validated, the gate review should establish a separate "Process Business Component" tracking code pursuant to IRC Section 41(d)(2)(C) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii). In parallel, organizations should refine their enterprise chart of accounts and inventory procurement systems to segregate prototype supplies from commercial production inventory. By establishing dedicated General Ledger accounts for consumed R&D prototype materials under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C) and customer-transferred experimental tooling under TG Missouri, 133 T.C. 278 (2009)—separate from standard raw materials, COGS, indirect "Prototype Overhead" excluded under the IRS ASC 730 Directive, and depreciable capital equipment—and tagging procurement orders with the specific business component name to distinguish "experimental runs" from "pilot production runs," taxpayers can demonstrate adherence to the statutory consumption rule.

From an operational engineering perspective, organizations should pair accounting segregation with periodic "Scrap and Fail" audits, component-level time tracking, and visual iteration logging. Because discarded, reworked, or destructively tested physical models provide strong evidence of technical uncertainty and non-depreciable material consumption, quarterly reviews of scrap logs and rework tickets should reconcile every failed prototype batch to its underlying failure analysis report, Engineering Change Order (ECO), and itemized material invoice. Accompanying these records with timestamped photographic logs of physical iterations (V1.0, V2.0, V3.0) and tagged version-control milestones for digital sandbox builds creates an objective, verifiable visual timeline of experimentation. Simultaneously, implementing project-specific time tracking for engineers, first-line supervisors, and production or quality personnel supporting prototype building and testing (or conducting contemporaneous quarterly project surveys where daily time tracking is unavailable) provides the empirical data needed to satisfy the 80% "substantially all" activity fraction under Little Sandy Coal and the business-component reporting rules of Form 6765 Section G. Finally, reviewing outbound vendor contracts under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e) and inbound customer agreements under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d) prior to execution, benchmarking internal costing practices against IRS Audit Techniques Guides, and evaluating upfront Research Credit Recordkeeping Agreements (RCRAs) with the IRS under Notice 2004-11 ensure that technical documentation translates seamlessly into a defensible federal tax claim.
